# Raw data management {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## Raw data is precious

Your raw data (e.g. FASTQ files) are the results of your experiment,\
and often expensive and labor-intensive to produce.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%" .box-blue .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
### Never delete it

- It remains your ground truth, even after you've produced processed files.

- It allows you and others to reproduce your results,
  and to re-analyze the data with new methods.

:::
::: {.column width="3%"}
:::
::: {.column width="30%" .box-amber .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}
### Keep multiple copies

- Ideally in at least two different physical locations.

- At OSC, never store it only in a scratch dir,
  where unused files are automatically deleted.

:::
::: {.column width="3%"}
:::
::: {.column width="30%" .box-teal .fragment data-fragment-index="3"}
### Share it publicly

- After publication.

- Required by most journals and funding agencies;
  has long been expected for sequencing data.

:::
:::

## Documenting and protecting raw data

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

### [Document it]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

- Keep track of data provenance:\
  when and from where did you get the data?

- Keep track of the metadata for each sample.

- Use standard, preferably plain-text file formats.

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

### [Protect it]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

- Consider making it read-only with file permissions
  _([bonus material](../bonus/data.qmd#making-your-data-read-only))_.

- After downloading or sharing key data,
  consider using "checksums" to check that files were transferred entirely
  _([bonus material](../bonus/data.qmd#checking-file-integrity-with-checksums))_.

:::
:::

## OSU data policies

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

### [Classification]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

- OSU data is classified as Public (S1), Internal (S2; default),
  Private (S3), or Restricted (S4).

- These levels determine where you may store data
  and which tools you may use with it
  (see: [IDP Calculator](https://it.osu.edu/data/institutional-data-policy){target="_blank"}
  & [approved AI tools](https://ai.osu.edu/resources-buckeyes/approved-ai-tools){target="_blank"}).

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

- E.g. plant, insect, and microbial omics data is typically S1--S2,
  which is fine for **regular OSC projects**.
  Identifiable human data is S4 and needs OSC's
  [Protected Data Service](https://www.osc.edu/resources/security_accessibility_and_policies){target="_blank"}.

:::

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="2" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}

### [Retention]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

- Keep research data for **at least 5 years after the project ends**,
  and at least until the student involved has graduated.

- Research data belongs to OSU, not to you:
  when you leave, you can generally take a copy,
  but the original stays at OSU,
  and further use requires agreement with your PI.

- See OSU's
  [Research Data](https://go.osu.edu/researchdatapolicy){target="_blank"}
  and [Institutional Data](https://go.osu.edu/idp){target="_blank"} policies.

:::
:::

# (Meta)data in spreadsheets {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## What data goes in spreadsheets?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

### [Omics data: mostly not]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

- Primary omics data, like FASTQ files or mass spectrometry raw files,
  comes in specialized formats
  and is far too large for a spreadsheet.

- Downstream results, like count or abundance tables,
  _may_ be delivered and/or stored in Excel files,
  but are best analyzed with code.

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

- So in omics projects, the main spreadsheet is your **sample metadata**,
  which you may enter by hand and your code then reads.

:::

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="2" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}

### [Field and lab data: often]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

- You may also have data from field or wet-lab experiments.

- Such data is often entered in spreadsheets as well ---
  the recommendations on the next slides apply to it too.

:::
:::

## Spreadsheet recommendations

Entering (meta)data in Excel is fine,
as long as code can read the spreadsheet without manual cleanup.
Some recommendations based on The Turing Way's
[Data Organisation in Spreadsheets](https://book.the-turing-way.org/reproducible-research/rdm/rdm-spreadsheets){target="_blank"}:

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

### [Structure]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

- No merged cells, colors, formatting, or comments to store information.
- No calculations (in raw data files).

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

- Only one value per cell.
- One row per sample, one column per variable, and a single header row.

:::
::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="2"}

- Need a place for notes?\
  Add columns or provide in a README.
- Export the final version as a CSV or TSV file.

:::

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="3" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="3"}

### [Content]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

- No spaces or special characters in sample and column names
  (`time_point`, not `Time point (days)`).
- Units in headers, if needed (`time_dpi`), not in cells (`10 dpi`).
- Dates as `YYYY-MM-DD` (e.g. `2026-11-04`).
- A single code for missing data\
  (e.g. `NA`, preferred over empty cells).

:::
:::

::: footer
:::

## Spreadsheet examples

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}

### [An OK example]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

The `garrigos/meta/metadata.tsv` file you've seen before:

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(gt)

# Shared styling for both tables on this slide
style_meta <- function(tbl) {
  tbl |>
    opt_table_font(font = "inherit", add = FALSE) |>
    tab_options(
      table.font.size = "0.93em",
      data_row.padding = px(3),
      column_labels.font.weight = "bold"
    )
}

meta_ok <- data.frame(
  sample_id = c("S82", "S75", "S78", "S84", "S76"),
  time = "10dpi",
  treatment = c("cathemerium", "cathemerium", "control", "control", "relictum")
)

gt(meta_ok) |>
  style_meta()
```

<hr style="height:50pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-note .quiz .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
#### What problem can you find here?
:::

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="2" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::

::: {.column width="54%" .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}

### [A problematic example]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
meta_bad <- data.frame(
  id = c("S82", "S75", "S78", "S84", "S76"),
  date = c("8/14/2026", "2026-08-14", "Aug 14", "8/14/2026", "8/14/2026"),
  time = c("10 dpi", "", "10 dpi", "10 dpi", "10 dpi"),
  treatment = c(
    "cathemerium",
    "Cathemerium",
    "control",
    "ctrl (low RNA yield)",
    "relictum"
  )
)

gt(meta_bad) |>
  cols_label(
    id = "Sample ID",
    date = "Collected",
    time = "Time point (days)",
    treatment = "Treatment"
  ) |>
  tab_spanner("Sample", columns = c(id, date)) |>
  tab_spanner("Infection", columns = c(time, treatment)) |>
  tab_style(cell_fill("#FFF3B0"), locations = cells_body(rows = 3)) |>
  tab_source_note("Yellow = sequenced twice") |>
  style_meta()
```

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-note .quiz}
#### And what problems can you find here?
:::

<!-----
<details><summary> {{< fa square-check >}} &nbsp; &nbsp; _Click for the answer_</summary>

- A second, merged header row (`Sample`, `Infection`)
- Spaces and special characters in the column names
- Information stored only as a background color (the yellow row):
  add a column like `n_seq_runs` instead
- Dates in different, ambiguous formats instead of `YYYY-MM-DD`
- An empty cell for a missing value (`S75`), instead of `NA`
- Units in cells (`10 dpi`), and different from the header (`days`)
- Inconsistent labels: `Cathemerium` vs. `cathemerium`, and `ctrl` vs. `control`
- Two values in one cell: put the RNA yield note in a separate column

</details>
------>

:::
:::

::: footer
:::

## Spreadsheet pitfall

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="7%"}

:::
::: {.column width="86%"}

::: callout-warning
#### Excel turns gene names into dates

- Excel converts text that **looks like** a date:
  _SEPT2_ and _MARCH1_ become `2-Sep` and `1-Mar`.

- About 20% of papers with gene lists in Excel files
  contained such errors [@ziemann2016],
  and several human genes were renamed because of it
  (_SEPT2_ is now _SEPTIN2_).

- To prevent this, set such columns to the "Text" format
  before entering or pasting data.
:::

:::
::: {.column width="7%"}

:::
:::

# Sharing data {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## Sharing is required

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

### [Public access]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

> By the end of 2025, all federally-funded research must make articles and data publicly available immediately upon journal publication with no waiting periods allowed.
>
> --- [Federal Research Policy Guide](https://research.osu.edu/federal-research-policy-guide-public-access-requirements){target="_blank"}
> from OSU's [ERIK](https://erik.osu.edu/){target="_blank"}

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

### [Data Management Plans]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

DMPs specify how you'll manage and share your data,
and major funders require them (NSF since 2011, NIH since 2023):

> A DMP is currently required for all competitive grant programs of the United States Department of Agriculture and the National Science Foundation.
>
> --- @grünwald2024

See the guidelines for
[USDA NIFA](https://www.nifa.usda.gov/grants/lifecycle/pre-award/data-management-plans){target="_blank"}
and [NSF](https://www.nsf.gov/funding/data-management-plan){target="_blank"} grants.

:::
:::

## Platforms for sharing data

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%" .box-blue .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
### NCBI

- **Raw reads** go to the
  [SRA](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sra){target="_blank"}
  (or Europe's [ENA](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/browser/home){target="_blank"}).

- Also for genome assemblies and annotations.

- **Count tables** go to [GEO](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/){target="_blank"},
  which also uploads the reads to the SRA.

:::
::: {.column width="3%"}
:::
::: {.column width="30%" .box-amber .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}
### General repositories

- For other results and data.

- E.g. [Dryad](https://datadryad.org/){target="_blank"}
  and [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/){target="_blank"}.

- Increasingly required by journals.

:::
::: {.column width="3%"}
:::
::: {.column width="30%" .box-teal .fragment data-fragment-index="3"}
### Code

- GitHub (or GitLab, Bitbucket), ideally with a DOI via Zenodo.

- Some journals also require code in a general repository,
  where it may get a manual quality check.

:::
:::

. . .

<br>

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
[OSU's Research Commons](https://library.osu.edu/researchcommons){target="_blank"}
has [data sharing guides](https://guides.osu.edu/rdm-best-practice/how-to-share){target="_blank"} and
[offers consultations](https://library.osu.edu/research-data){target="_blank"}.
:::

## A DOI for your GitHub repo with Zenodo

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

### [Why?]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

- A GitHub repo can be changed or deleted at any time:
  a poor permanent reference in a paper.

- Zenodo, a general repository run by CERN,
  can archive a snapshot of your repo and give it a citable DOI.

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

### [How?]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

- Connect [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/){target="_blank"} to your GitHub account,
  and switch on archiving for a (public) repo.

- Zenodo then archives each GitHub "release" of the repo with its own DOI,
  plus a "concept DOI" that always points to the latest version.

- Step-by-step instructions are in this week's
  [self-study exercise](w11a_data.qmd){target="_blank"} and in GA5.

:::
:::

# Syncing OSC and local files {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## Should I keep my OSC and local dirs synced?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

### [Syncing strategy]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

Fully automatic syncing like with OneDrive or Dropbox isn't possible ---
and with large OSC data, you may not want it. Instead:

- Sync version-controlled files via Git/GitHub.
- Periodically sync other files with the transfer methods discussed on
  the lecture page and this [bonus page](/bonus/data.qmd).

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

### [Or: work in one place]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

- Running analyses both at OSC and locally makes syncing a hassle.

- So for projects that need OSC,\
  consider doing **all** your analyses there.

- Your local computer (and/or OneDrive/Teams) can then hold
  an entirely **separate** set of files, like the manuscript.

:::
:::

# Side note:<br>Why you should prefer relative paths {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## Absolute vs. relative paths

::: {.callout-note .quiz}
#### Absolute paths don't depend on your working dir --- so what could be a disadvantage of using them?
:::

## Absolute vs. relative paths

![](../img/proj-dirs-2-2025.png){fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="A diagram of two project dir hierarchies."}

<hr style="height:10pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: legend2
Absolute and relative paths to a FASTQ file in two project dirs.\
The relative paths start from the project's top-level dir
(`~` is your Home dir).
:::

::: footer
:::

## Absolute vs. relative paths

![](../img/proj-dirs-3-2025.png){fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="A diagram of two project dir hierarchies."}

<hr style="height:10pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: legend2
After moving both projects into `OneDrive`,\
the absolute path has changed, but the relative path has not.
:::

::: footer
:::

## Absolute vs. relative paths

::: {.callout-note .quiz}
#### Absolute paths don't depend on your working dir --- so what could be a disadvantage of using them?
Absolute paths:

- Break when you **move** your entire project dir
- Don't generally work **across computers**

Relative paths keep working in these scenarios,\
**as long as** you always use the project's top-level dir as your working dir.
:::

## Relative paths in practice

::: {.callout-note .quiz}
#### Would last week's relative paths still work after moving dirs?

Last week, you referred to input files from `week10` with relative paths like
`../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz`. Would these still work after moving:

- `week10` into a new dir?
- Your entire personal dir?

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

<!-----
<details><summary> {{< fa square-check >}} &nbsp; &nbsp; _Click for the answer_</summary>

- Moving only `week10` breaks them:
  `..` would now point to the new dir, which has no `garrigos` dir inside it.
- Moving your entire personal dir keeps them working,
  since `week10` and `garrigos` move together.

This is why it's best to keep all files for a project, including its raw data,
inside the project's top-level dir, so that relative paths never need to leave it.
(When multiple projects use the same data,
you can use symbolic links: see the [bonus material](../bonus/data.qmd#symbolic-links).)

</details>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />
------>
